Senior living communities, particularly those with memory care or higher levels of support, can have waitlists, and if a move becomes urgent before you've started looking, options narrow dramatically. If a community seems like the right fit, get on the list now even if a move isn't imminent, visit in person, and learn the costs, since many options are private pay. It is research and relationship-building, and it commits no one to anything.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: When a Move Seems Like It's Coming

plan-ahead.q: Is there a point when it's too late to sign a will or power of attorney?
alts: memory loss too late to sign power of attorney
Can someone with early dementia still update their will?
how long does an estate planning attorney take

plan-ahead.a: Yes, there can be. A person's ability to sign legal documents can be affected by cognitive decline, and once that threshold is crossed, the window to create or update powers of attorney, wills and trusts may close. If documents are missing or outdated, now is the time. A Washington estate planning attorney can typically move through the process in a matter of weeks, at a modest cost relative to the protection.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: When a Move Seems Like It's Coming

plan-ahead.q: Should I have my house appraised before I plan a move?
alts: appraisal before downsizing
Why get a home value now if we're not selling yet?

Should we find out what Mom's house is worth before she moves?
plan-ahead.a: It often helps. If the home may be sold to fund care, knowing the likely net proceeds changes the financial picture, and knowing what preparation it needs leaves time to get bids and choose what to fix. An appraisal from a Washington State certified appraiser gives an independent, defensible figure to plan around, useful for tax and estate purposes. Online estimates can be significantly off.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: When a Move Seems Like It's Coming

plan-ahead.q: What goes wrong when families wait until a crisis to plan?
alts: cost of not planning ahead for aging
Why plan before a health emergency?
What happens if we don't plan and Dad suddenly gets sick?
rushed home sale after a crisis
plan-ahead.a: Typically: rushed real estate decisions, legal gaps, family conflict and missed opportunities. A home sold quickly to fund care often hits the market before it's ready, and in Western Washington that gap can reach tens of thousands of dollars. Without legal authority in place, family may be unable to access bank accounts or sign real estate documents. And some options are only available with lead time.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: Why Planning Early Makes Such a Difference

plan-ahead.q: How far ahead should I start planning to sell my home before a move?
alts: when to start preparing to sell before assisted living
senior home sale planning timeline
how early to plan a downsizing sale
plan-ahead.a: As early as possible. Even if a move is months away, early planning allows time for a property assessment, conversations about preparation and realistic expectations, which reduces pressure and gives the family more control over timing. Senior transition sales often have to line up with assisted living waitlists, care transitions and health events, and a home lived in for decades usually needs more preparation.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: How Senior Transition Sales Differ From Ordinary Home Sales

plan-ahead.q: Do I need to clean out the house before getting it valued?
alts: clean out before appraisal
Should we empty Mom's house before the appraiser comes?
home valuation with belongings still inside
declutter before getting the house valued
plan-ahead.a: Not necessarily. A certified appraiser or real estate professional can usually assess a home in its current condition, with belongings still in place. Cleaning out before listing may help, but valuation often comes first, and valuing the home as it is usually shows which repairs are worth doing. Cleanout often happens in stages alongside other preparation.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: Downsizing & Preparing for a Transition

plan-ahead.q: Which repairs are worth doing before I sell my longtime home?
alts: repairs before selling a senior's home
Should I update the kitchen before selling?
sell house as-is or fix it up
what to fix before listing an older house
plan-ahead.a: Safety, water, roof and major mechanical issues tend to matter most; cosmetic upgrades vary by market, and many updates do not return their cost. Many homes sell well as-is, and updating is rarely all-or-nothing. Selling as-is can simplify the process, while targeted preparation may improve the outcome. Getting a valuation in current condition first helps show which repairs make sense.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: Preparing a Home for Sale During a Transition

plan-ahead.q: How do I start downsizing after 40 years in the same house?
alts: where to begin downsizing
too much stuff to move to a smaller place
how long does downsizing take
downsizing tips for seniors moving
plan-ahead.a: Start small: a single category such as papers or photos, or one room, and build momentum from there. Timelines vary widely; some families work over many weeks or months, while others compress the process when a move or health event creates urgency. Small, consistent sessions usually feel most manageable, and a senior move manager can help when the work feels too large to handle alone.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: Downsizing & Preparing for a Transition

plan-ahead.q: Will I owe capital gains tax when I sell my home to move into care?
alts: home sale exclusion after moving to assisted living
capital gains selling house after moving to a nursing home
250000 exclusion if I've been in a care facility
taxes on selling a longtime family home washington
plan-ahead.a: Possibly not, up to a limit. A seller who owned and lived in the home at least two of the five years before the sale can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly. Someone who became unable to care for themselves and moved into a licensed care facility may still qualify if they lived in the home at least one of the five years. Heirs who inherit receive a stepped-up basis instead. A CPA or financial planner should be part of the conversation before listing.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: Senior Housing Transitions & Downsizing in Washington State

plan-ahead.q: What are the costliest mistakes families make when deciding what to do with the house?
alts: avoid costly mistakes with a parent's home
What should we not do first with Mom's house?
biggest mistakes in a senior home sale
Should we start repairs before deciding anything?
plan-ahead.a: The most expensive mistakes come from acting before authority is confirmed, guessing at value, or making large repairs without input. Slow down and assemble the right team first: usually an attorney, a real estate professional and often a CPA, with a housing advisor and move manager in senior situations. Families typically choose to sell, keep, rent or transfer the home, depending on care costs, family goals, taxes and timing.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: What Should We Do First?

plan-ahead.q: If I move into a 62+ community, can my younger spouse stay after I die?
alts: 62 plus community younger spouse rules
Can my 58-year-old wife live with me in a 62+ community?
difference between 55+ and 62+ communities
younger spouse in a senior community after a death
plan-ahead.a: Generally not in a 62+ community. Every resident must be 62 or older, and the federal rules allow only narrow exceptions, such as people who lived there before September 13, 1988 and staff; a younger spouse is not one of them. A 55+ community is more flexible: each sets its own rules, and a younger spouse may be able to stay after a death in one community but not another. Read the written age policy.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: 55+ Communities in Washington: What Families Should Know

plan-ahead.q: Is a community marketed to retirees automatically a legal 55+ community?
alts: age-targeted vs age-restricted community
How does a community qualify as 55 and over?
Can a retirement community turn away younger buyers?
55+ community 80 percent rule
plan-ahead.a: No. To be age-restricted, a 55+ community must have at least one resident 55 or older in at least 80 percent of occupied homes, publish and follow age policies, and verify ages with surveys updated at least every two years. A community only marketed to retirees without meeting these tests is age-targeted, not age-restricted, and cannot turn away younger buyers or renters.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: 55+ Communities in Washington: What Families Should Know

plan-ahead.q: Is there a way to keep my house and savings out of probate?
alts: Can probate be avoided?
how to avoid probate washington
How can I make sure my kids don't have to go through probate?
ways to skip probate on my house
what can I do now so my family avoids probate
plan-ahead.a: Yes, with planning. A will usually leads to probate. A funded trust, one that actually holds the property, can pass it to heirs without probate, and a recorded transfer on death deed, joint tenancy with right of survivorship, or a community property agreement can also pass property outside probate. Beneficiary designations on life insurance, retirement accounts and payable-on-death accounts pass outside the will. There is no universal winner, so an estate planning attorney can help evaluate which approach fits.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: The Legal Documents That Matter Most

plan-ahead.q: What is a payable-on-death or transfer-on-death account?
alts: What is a payable-on-death (POD) or transfer-on-death (TOD) account?
POD account meaning
How does a payable on death bank account work?
TOD account vs will
plan-ahead.a: It is a bank or investment account with a named beneficiary, marked payable on death (POD) or transfer on death (TOD). Like the beneficiary on a life insurance policy or retirement account, the designation passes the account directly to that person at death, outside the will, and in most cases it controls whatever the will says. Review these designations regularly to make sure they still reflect your wishes, especially after a divorce, a death in the family or another major life change.
plan-ahead.pathTitle: The Legal Documents That Matter Most

aging-parent.q: How do I bring up moving to assisted living with my mom without upsetting her?
alts: how do I talk to my dad about getting more help
my parent gets defensive when I mention senior living, how do I start
talking to aging parents about care options
what do I say to my mother about not living alone anymore
aging-parent.a: Start from your parent's wishes, not your worries. An opener like "I want to make sure we understand what you'd want if things changed" lands better than "I'm worried about you living alone." Pick a quiet, unhurried moment, not a crisis or a family gathering, and don't try to cover everything at once. Listen more than you talk; many parents have thought about this more than their children realize.
aging-parent.pathTitle: How do I have this conversation with my parent?

aging-parent.q: What if every conversation with my parent about care turns into an argument?
alts: my dad refuses to discuss moving, who can help
family keeps fighting about mom's care conversation
someone to help talk to my parent about care
mediator for talking with elderly parent
aging-parent.a: Bring in a neutral third party. A geriatric care manager, social worker, or family mediator can facilitate these conversations when family dynamics make them difficult, and that is a normal, legitimate resource. You also don't need to settle everything at once: one conversation about what your parent would want if they needed more help is enough to start.
aging-parent.pathTitle: How do I have this conversation with my parent?

aging-parent.q: What should we talk about with my parents before there's a health crisis?
alts: what to discuss with aging parents ahead of time
planning conversation with mom and dad about the future
early planning aging parent checklist
what should I ask my dad while he's still healthy
aging-parent.a: Cover what your parent wants if they can no longer live independently; whether they'd prefer staying home with help, moving in with family, or a care community; where key documents are kept; who they want making decisions if they can't; and whether their finances support those preferences. The goal isn't to convince them to move. It's to understand their wishes so the right people have authority if it's ever needed.
aging-parent.pathTitle: Starting early planning conversations

aging-parent.q: How do I know if my mom can't live alone anymore?
alts: signs my elderly parent needs more help
is it time for my dad to move out of his house
parent not safe living alone signs
how to tell if mom needs assisted living
aging-parent.a: Ask some honest questions. Is the home genuinely safe, or just familiar? Does your parent need help with bathing, dressing, or medications? Are memory concerns growing rather than stable? Is loneliness becoming a health issue? What would happen after a fall or a hospital stay? An Aging Life Care Manager can do a thorough professional assessment and translate it into a clear picture of the right level of care.
aging-parent.pathTitle: How to Choose Senior Housing

aging-parent.q: When is it time for memory care for my dad with dementia?
alts: signs mom needs memory care
dementia parent too much to handle at home what now
memory care when to move
is it too soon to move my mother to memory care
aging-parent.a: Common signs include wandering that creates real safety risk; repeated incidents like falls, leaving the stove on, or getting lost; agitation or nighttime disruption beyond what family or home caregivers can safely manage; needs that have outgrown assisted living; and a primary caregiver whose own health is suffering. The decision is rarely clean, and an Aging Life Care Manager can assess where your parent actually is.
aging-parent.pathTitle: Memory Care Costs

aging-parent.q: What's the difference between independent living and assisted living?
alts: independent living vs assisted living
does independent living include help with bathing
my mom needs some help, is independent living enough
which is right for my dad, independent or assisted living
aging-parent.a: Independent living is for seniors who are largely self-sufficient: it offers community, dining, and maintenance-free living, but no care services. Assisted living adds personal care. In Washington it is licensed by DSHS for seven or more residents, with help with daily activities and staff available around the clock. If your parent already needs hands-on help with bathing or dressing, independent living alone may not be enough.
aging-parent.pathTitle: What types of senior housing exist?

aging-parent.q: How is an adult family home different from assisted living?
alts: adult family home vs assisted living washington
is an AFH smaller than assisted living
difference between AFH and ALF
aging-parent.a: Mainly scale and setting. An adult family home is a private house serving up to six residents (occasionally eight) with a live-in or round-the-clock caregiver. An assisted living facility is a licensed building, often with dozens to hundreds of apartments, shift staff, and communal dining. Washington licenses the two under different laws, with different building requirements and inspection rules.
aging-parent.pathTitle: What is an adult family home — and what is it called in your state?

aging-parent.q: When does my parent need a nursing home instead of an adult family home?
alts: nursing home or adult family home for my dad
can an adult family home handle medical needs
when is a nursing home necessary
mom has medical needs, does she have to go to a nursing home
aging-parent.a: Generally when they need licensed nurses on staff, such as for complex medical management or rehab after a hospital stay. Adult family homes usually are not staffed by licensed nurses. But through nurse delegation, a registered nurse can train and authorize caregivers to do some nursing tasks, which lets many people with medical needs stay in an adult family home.
aging-parent.pathTitle: How to Choose Between Care Settings: A Guide for Washington Families

aging-parent.q: Can a caregiver give my mom insulin shots at home or in an adult family home?
alts: nurse delegation washington
can a caregiver do wound care for my dad
does mom need a nurse for insulin injections
caregiver allowed to give medications adult family home
aging-parent.a: Often yes, through Washington's Nurse Delegation Program. A registered nurse trains and authorizes a credentialed caregiver to do specific nursing tasks for a specific client, such as insulin, oral medications, wound care, or catheter care. Your parent's condition must be stable and predictable. Some tasks can never be delegated, including injections other than insulin and sterile procedures. It is not used in nursing homes.
aging-parent.pathTitle: The Nurse Delegation Program in Washington State: What Families Need to Know

aging-parent.q: Who pays for nurse delegation if my dad is on Medicaid?
alts: does medicaid cover nurse delegation
cost of delegating nurse washington
how often does the delegating nurse visit
nurse delegation paid by DSHS
aging-parent.a: For eligible Medicaid long-term care clients, Washington's Medicaid program covers the delegating nurse's assessments, training, and oversight visits, so the family does not pay them out of pocket. The nurse visits at least every 90 days to monitor your parent and check in with the caregiver. A DSHS case manager, a home health agency, or an Aging Life Care Manager can help decide whether delegation fits.
aging-parent.pathTitle: The Nurse Delegation Program in Washington State: What Families Need to Know

aging-parent.q: What does memory care provide that regular assisted living doesn't?
alts: what is memory care
memory care vs assisted living for dementia
is memory care locked
what's included in memory care for my mom
aging-parent.a: Memory care is built for people with Alzheimer's or other dementia: secured entrances and exits, enclosed outdoor spaces, layouts that reduce confusion, caregivers trained in dementia care, structured routines, and supervision that never fully switches off. It is often located inside an assisted living community. Before choosing, ask whether medication management and one-on-one behavioral support are included or cost extra.
aging-parent.pathTitle: Memory Care Costs

aging-parent.q: Does going into a nursing home mean my dad will never come home?
alts: is a nursing home stay permanent
short term rehab nursing home after surgery
mom going to skilled nursing after hospital, will she come back home
temporary nursing home stay
aging-parent.a: No, not necessarily. Many nursing home stays are short-term rehab after a hip or knee replacement, a stroke, a serious infection, or a new medical condition, with the goal of returning home or moving to an assisted living facility or adult family home. Ask from day one what the goals of the stay are, what milestones must be reached before going home, and what support will be needed afterward.
aging-parent.pathTitle: Short-Term Nursing Home Stays in Washington State: What Families Need to Know

aging-parent.q: Who do I call if I'm worried about my mom's care in a nursing home?
alts: report nursing home neglect washington
nursing home ombudsman washington
complaint about my dad's nursing home
elder abuse hotline washington
aging-parent.a: Washington's Long-Term Care Ombuds Program has independent advocates who investigate complaints in nursing homes and help residents and families resolve concerns, at no cost. To report suspected abuse or neglect of a vulnerable adult in a long-term care setting, call the DSHS EndHarm hotline at 1-866-363-4276, available 24 hours a day.
aging-parent.pathTitle: Nursing Homes in Washington State: What Families Need to Know

aging-parent.q: Does a senior placement advisor cost my family anything?
alts: who pays senior living advisor
are placement agencies free
senior living advisor fees washington
how do placement advisors get paid
aging-parent.a: Usually not. Senior living advisors are typically paid by the communities and care providers in their network, not by the family. In Washington, an elder placement agency must give you a written disclosure statement before making a referral, including how its fee from a provider is computed, and must tell you the amount of that fee if you ask.
aging-parent.pathTitle: The Senior Housing Guide

aging-parent.q: My mom only has Social Security. Is there affordable senior housing for her?
alts: low income senior housing
subsidized apartments for seniors on fixed income
section 202 senior housing how it works
cheap housing for my elderly parent
aging-parent.a: Yes, but expect waitlists of months or even years, so apply early. Programs include HUD Section 202 senior housing, where residents generally pay about 30% of adjusted income in rent, tax-credit (LIHTC) buildings, Section 8 vouchers, and state and local programs. These are housing, not care: meals and personal care usually aren't included. The local housing authority and Area Agency on Aging are the usual places to start.
aging-parent.pathTitle: Affordable Senior Housing

aging-parent.q: Where do I report a problem at my dad's adult family home?
alts: complaint about an adult family home washington
DSHS complaint line adult family home
worried about care at mom's AFH who do I call
adult family home ombudsman
aging-parent.a: In an emergency, call 911. Concerns about care go to the DSHS Complaint Resolution Unit at 1-800-562-6078 (TTY 1-800-737-7931), and every home must post the complaint number where residents and visitors can see it. The Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program also offers free, independent help to residents and families.
aging-parent.pathTitle: How to Choose an Adult Family Home in Washington

aging-parent.q: An adult family home quoted my mom "Level 3." How do I compare that to other homes?
alts: adult family home care levels pricing
AFH base rate plus care level
why are adult family home prices so different
what does level 3 mean at an adult family home
aging-parent.a: You can't compare levels directly. Many homes charge private-pay residents a base rate plus a care-level charge, and each home defines its own levels, so "Level 3" at one home tells you nothing about Level 3 at another. Ask each home for the total monthly cost at your parent's level of care, what raises the rate, and how much notice it gives before a change. Get it in writing.
aging-parent.pathTitle: How to Choose an Adult Family Home in Washington

aging-parent.q: My mom has dementia. What should I look for in an adult family home?
alts: adult family home for dementia
AFH dementia specialty designation
best questions for memory care adult family home
dementia care in a small home washington
aging-parent.a: Look for a home with a dementia specialty designation, which means its staff completed the DSHS training for it. On the tour, ask which designations the home holds, how many caregivers are on duty overnight and whether they're awake, and whether the home works with a delegating nurse. The home's Disclosure of Services also states what it does and does not do.
aging-parent.pathTitle: How to Choose an Adult Family Home in Washington

aging-parent.q: If my dad pays privately and runs out of money, can he stay in his adult family home on Medicaid?
alts: what happens when private pay runs out adult family home
switch from private pay to medicaid AFH
will the adult family home keep my mom on medicaid
medicaid bed adult family home
aging-parent.a: It depends on the home, so ask before moving in: does it have a Medicaid contract, and can a private-pay resident stay on Medicaid if savings run out? Most Washington adult family homes hold a Medicaid contract, but many limit how many Medicaid residents they take, so a contract is not the same as an open Medicaid bed.
aging-parent.pathTitle: How to Choose an Adult Family Home in Washington

aging-parent.q: What's included in the monthly price of an adult family home?
alts: what does an adult family home cover
adult family home included services
does AFH rate include meals and medications
what am I paying for at an adult family home
aging-parent.a: Typically room and board, personal care, meals, medication management, and 24-hour supervision. Each home sets its own private-pay rate, and no survey publishes them. For Medicaid residents, DSHS pays the home about $4,030 to $8,495 a month (rates effective July 1, 2026), depending on county and care level.
aging-parent.pathTitle: Adult Family Homes

aging-parent.q: If Medicaid pays for my mom's adult family home, does she still have to pay anything?
alts: medicaid resident share of cost adult family home
personal needs allowance washington AFH
does mom's social security go to the adult family home
out of pocket on medicaid adult family home

So the family's out-of-pocket is usually the resident's income, not the DSHS daily rate. That rate is what the state pays the home, and it is what makes a home willing to accept a Medicaid placement at a given care level.
aging-parent.pathTitle: What It Costs to Live in an Adult Family Home, by City and County

adult family home medicaid daily rate 2026

average price of assisted living in WA

price of a semi private room nursing home WA
how much is skilled nursing a month

why is the assisted living bill higher than quoted

Many communities add fees for care levels, medications, and transportation, and most assisted living communities charge more as care needs grow. Also ask what is included (meals, laundry, activities, transportation), whether there is a second-person fee or a move-in fee or deposit, and how often rates increase and by how much.

aging-parent.q: Will an adult family home cost less than assisted living for my dad?
alts: adult family home vs assisted living cost
AFH cost compared to assisted living
is a small care home less expensive
aging-parent.a: Often, but compare at the same level of care. The site's planning figures are about $6,500 a month for an adult family home (an estimate) and a $7,546 Washington median for assisted living. Adult family homes set their own private-pay rates, so the real comparison is each home's all-in monthly cost at your parent's care level.

use home equity to pay for care

In the site's illustrative example, a $600,000 home with a $100,000 mortgage and $40,000 in closing and preparation costs nets about $460,000, which is roughly 5 years of assisted living at about $7,550 a month. aging-parent.q: Will Medicare pay for my mom to live in assisted living or a nursing home long-term?
alts: does medicare cover long term care
medicare assisted living coverage
who pays for a nursing home if not medicare
medicare custodial care
aging-parent.a: No. Medicare covers short-term skilled nursing and rehab after a formal inpatient hospital stay of at least three days, not long-term custodial care. Long-term care is usually paid privately (savings, retirement accounts, home equity), by long-term care insurance, by VA Aid & Attendance for eligible veterans and surviving spouses, or by Washington Medicaid (Apple Health) for those who qualify.
aging-parent.pathTitle: Paying for care

aging-parent.q: My mom has a long-term care insurance policy. What should I check?
alts: how to use long term care insurance for my dad
long term care insurance elimination period
filing a long term care insurance claim
parent's LTC policy what to look for
aging-parent.a: Find the policy now and learn three things: the elimination period (how long before benefits kick in), the daily benefit amount, and how to file a claim. Policies vary significantly. Long-term care insurance is one of the usual ways families pay for care, alongside savings, retirement accounts, home equity, veterans benefits and Apple Health. Most assisted living residents pay privately or with long-term care insurance.
aging-parent.pathTitle: Paying for care

aging-parent.q: Can my dad get VA benefits to help pay for assisted living?

veterans benefit for assisted living
can my mom get VA benefits as a widow
aid and attendance net worth limit 2026
aging-parent.a: Possibly. The VA's Aid & Attendance benefit is an add-on to the VA pension for veterans and surviving spouses who need help with daily activities. Because it is part of the pension, wartime service and income and net-worth limits apply ($163,699 net worth limit through Nov. 30, 2026). A VA-accredited representative, claims agent, or attorney can help with the application.
aging-parent.pathTitle: What does my parent qualify for?

aging-parent.q: What is WA Cares, and can it help pay for care?

aging-parent.a: WA Cares is Washington's mandatory public long-term care insurance program for workers. It began collecting premiums in 2023 and started paying benefits in July 2026. Eligible workers who paid in and meet the benefit triggers can receive up to $36,500 in lifetime benefits, growing with inflation, for personal care, facility care, transportation, meal delivery, and home modifications. It supplements Medicaid rather than replacing it.
aging-parent.pathTitle: Medicaid & Long-Term Care in Washington State: What Families Need to Know

aging-parent.q: How much money can my mom have and still qualify for Medicaid long-term care in Washington?

apple health long term care resource limit
how much savings can you keep on medicaid WA

aging-parent.a: The asset limit is $2,000 for a single person, or $3,000 for a married couple who both receive care. A primary residence (within a home equity limit), one vehicle, personal belongings, and certain other assets are exempt. If one spouse stays at home, that spouse can keep a share of the couple's assets, up to $162,660 in 2026. Your parent must also meet a separate medical need test.

For nursing home care there is no fixed income cap: someone whose income is less than the cost of their care may still qualify, and most of their income then goes toward that cost.

That spend-down is how the system is designed, not a failure of planning. How the money is spent matters: money spent on care is treated differently than money transferred to family members, which can trigger a penalty.

Equity is your parent's share of the value minus the mortgage and other debts on it, so an accurate, documented value matters if the house is near the limit.

Washington seeks to recover what it paid for federally funded long-term services received at age 55 or older, and state-funded services at any age, from the estate. That reaches non-probate assets too, such as a house passing by transfer on death deed, and life estates. Recovery is deferred while a spouse, a child under 21, or a blind or disabled child survives, and hardship waivers exist.

Call the homeowner's insurer, because policies often limit coverage once a home is unoccupied for a set period. Keep the heat on in winter, forward the mail, and have someone check the house regularly.

Medicare pays the full cost for days 1 to 20; days 21 to 100 carry a $217-a-day copayment in 2026; after day 100 coverage ends, and it can end sooner if daily skilled care is no longer needed. Your parent must have been a formal inpatient for at least three days in a row and generally enter a Medicare-certified facility within 30 days.

Ask the hospital in writing whether your parent is an inpatient or under observation, ideally before agreeing to a skilled nursing placement.
aging-parent.pathTitle: Short-Term Nursing Home Stays in Washington State: What Families Need to Know

He can stay in the hospital while the review is decided without paying for those extra days, other than usual deductibles or coinsurance.

In the first weeks, protect the house and keep every option open.

Without durable wording, it won't help once your parent can't sign.

If these aren't in place, act while your parent still has capacity; an elder law attorney can often prepare them within days.

If both are affected, both need someone with authority to sign.

aging-parent.q: Will my mom lose the capital gains exclusion if she's been in care for a while before we sell?

For a parent who moved into a licensed care facility because they could no longer care for themselves, one of those five years is enough, and time in the facility counts as living in the home. Washington's capital gains tax does not apply to real estate.

Ask a CPA to compare before listing.

estate.a: It is better to wait. Letting heirs or family members take items before a proper inventory creates disputes and legal complications. Nothing should be distributed until the estate has been properly administered and its debts identified and paid, and distributing too early can make the executor personally liable. Coordinate with the heirs about personal and sentimental items first, then plan the cleanout.
estate.pathTitle: What Should an Executor Do First With a House?

estate.q: Do I have to tell Social Security my dad died?

who to notify when a parent dies
Do we have to give back mom's Social Security payment after she passed?
who should the executor notify in the first two weeks
estate.a: Yes. If the person was receiving Social Security, notify the Social Security Administration promptly, because benefits paid after the date of death must be returned. In the first week or two also notify Medicare and any supplemental insurance, the banks and investment firms, and the post office so mail is forwarded somewhere you can watch for bills and statements.
estate.pathTitle: Your First 30 Days as Executor

estate.q: The will says the house should be sold. Can I just sell it?
alts: will says sell the house do I still need probate
I'm named executor in my mom's will, can I list her house now?
does the will give the executor authority to sell

estate.a: Not yet. Even when the will directs a sale, the executor generally needs court-issued authority first. The will states the person's wishes, but the court must appoint you and issue letters testamentary before you can sign a listing, accept an offer or transfer title, and the title company will require that court paperwork before closing. You can secure, insure and prepare the house in the meantime.
estate.pathTitle: Can an Executor Sell a House Before Probate in Washington?

estate.q: What are letters testamentary?
alts: letters testamentary meaning
What document proves I'm the executor?
letters of administration vs letters testamentary
What paper does the title company want from the executor?
estate.a: Letters testamentary are the court document proving that a personal representative named in a will has been appointed. Banks, title companies and buyers ask for a recently certified copy before dealing with the estate. When there is no will, or no named executor can serve, the court issues letters of administration instead, which give the appointed administrator the same authority over the house.
estate.pathTitle: Washington Probate & Estate Glossary

estate.q: How do I get letters testamentary in Washington?
alts: how to get appointed executor Washington
Where do I file to become personal representative for my dad's estate?
petition for probate Washington superior court
steps to get court authority as executor
estate.a: The person named in the will, usually through a probate attorney, petitions the superior court and files the original will. The petitioner may choose any Washington county. When the court admits the will and appoints the personal representative, the clerk issues letters testamentary. Until then, the executor can secure and insure the house but cannot sell it.
estate.pathTitle: Who Has Authority to Sell Probate Property?

estate.q: How long does it take to get authority to sell the house after filing for probate?
alts: how long to get letters testamentary Washington
wait time for executor appointment
When will the court let me sell mom's house?
how fast does Washington appoint a personal representative
estate.a: It depends on the case. Washington lets the court admit a will and appoint the executor as soon as the petition is presented, heirs are notified after the appointment, and letters issue once the executor's oath is filed and any required bond is posted. In an uncontested case the wait is mostly preparing the petition and the county's processing time. A contested will or a dispute over who should serve can take months.
estate.pathTitle: Can an Executor Sell a House Before Probate in Washington?

estate.q: Who is in charge of the estate if my dad died without a will?
alts: no will who becomes administrator Washington
Mom died intestate, who can sell her house?

who handles an estate when there's no will
estate.a: The court appoints an administrator in a set order of priority: the surviving spouse or registered domestic partner first, then next of kin. A nonresident may serve by appointing a local agent. Once appointed, the administrator receives letters of administration and has the same authority over the house as an executor named in a will.
estate.pathTitle: Who Has Authority to Sell Probate Property?

estate.q: I'm the only heir. Can I sell my mother's house without going to court?

Does being the beneficiary let me sell dad's house?
can next of kin sell a house without being appointed
estate.a: Not if the house was in her name alone. Only the personal representative can sell a house that goes through probate, and only after the superior court appoints them and issues letters. Being an heir does not give that authority, and neither does being named executor on its own. You would first need a court appointment; then, with nonintervention powers, the personal representative can sell without a court order.
estate.pathTitle: Washington Probate Deadlines & Key Rules

estate under $100,000 do we need probate
Can a small estate skip probate if there's a house?

estate.a: No. Washington's small estate affidavit can be used when the whole probate estate, including any real estate, is worth $100,000 or less after liens, and 40 days have passed since the death. It lets a successor collect personal property such as bank accounts, but it cannot transfer real estate. So a house in the person's name alone usually means probate, however small the rest of the estate is.
estate.pathTitle: Washington Probate Deadlines & Key Rules

estate.q: Which county do I file probate in if my dad lived in a different county?
alts: where to file probate Washington
What court handles probate in Washington?
can I open probate in my own county
probate venue Washington county
Where is a probate petition filed?
which court do I file probate in
estate.a: In Washington, probate is filed in superior court, in any county the petitioner chooses. Within four months, a party can have the case moved to the county where the person lived. Most estates are then handled with little court involvement.
estate.pathTitle: Washington Probate Deadlines & Key Rules

estate.q: I have my mother's original will. What am I supposed to do with it?
alts: deadline to deliver will to court Washington
holding original will after death
Do I have to file dad's will with the court?
how long does executor have to file the will
estate.a: Deliver it. Anyone holding a person's original will must deliver it to the court or to the executor named in it within 30 days of learning of the death, and the named executor must deliver the original will to the court within 40 days of learning of the death. In Washington, probate is filed in superior court.
estate.pathTitle: Washington Probate Deadlines & Key Rules

estate.q: Does the executor have to tell the heirs that probate was opened?
alts: notice to heirs after appointment Washington
I never heard from the executor, were they supposed to notify me?
notice of appointment and pendency of probate
how soon must heirs be notified of probate
estate.a: Yes. Within 20 days of appointment, the personal representative must send notice to each heir, beneficiary under the will and nonprobate beneficiary whose address is reasonably known, saying the probate is open and who is in charge. If you never received one, it is reasonable to ask why.
estate.pathTitle: Washington Probate & Estate Glossary

estate.q: How does the executor notify my dad's creditors?
alts: notice to creditors Washington probate
how long do creditors have to file a claim
creditor claim period Washington
Do I have to publish a notice for dad's bills?
How long do creditors have to file a claim against the estate?
deadline for creditors to make a claim on an estate
estate.a: The personal representative publishes a notice to creditors once a week for three weeks in a legal newspaper, files it with the court, and mails it to known creditors, with a copy to the DSHS Office of Financial Recovery. Creditors then have four months after the first publication (or 30 days after a mailed notice, if later). If no notice is given, claims can be brought for up to 24 months after the death.
estate.pathTitle: Washington Probate & Estate Glossary

estate.q: Does the executor have to make an inventory of everything in the estate?
alts: probate inventory deadline Washington
Can I see the estate inventory as an heir?
inventory and appraisement three months
how do I get a copy of the estate inventory
estate.a: Yes. Within three months of appointment, unless the court allows longer, the personal representative prepares an inventory listing everything in the estate with its value as of the date of death. It is not filed with the court by default, but an heir, beneficiary or creditor with a filed claim who asks must be given a copy within 10 days.
estate.pathTitle: Washington Probate & Estate Glossary

estate.q: How long do I have to contest my parent's will in Washington?
alts: will contest deadline Washington
challenge a will time limit
I think dad's will is invalid, is it too late?
contesting a will undue influence deadline
estate.a: A will contest must be filed within four months after the will is admitted to probate or rejected, and the personal representative must be served within 90 days of filing. Common grounds include lack of capacity, undue influence or how the will was signed. Because the deadline is short, talk with a Washington probate attorney promptly.
estate.pathTitle: Washington Probate & Estate Glossary

estate.q: Who inherits my dad's house if he died without a will and my mom is still alive?
alts: intestate succession Washington spouse and children
no will who gets the house Washington
What does the surviving spouse get without a will?
Washington inheritance order without a will
estate.a: Washington's default rules decide. A surviving spouse or registered domestic partner receives all of the decedent's share of community property, and one-half of separate property if there are children or other descendants. The rest goes to descendants. How the house is classified, community or separate, can change the answer, so the estate's attorney should confirm it.
estate.pathTitle: Washington Probate & Estate Glossary

estate.q: What assets don't have to go through probate?
alts: non-probate assets list
Do life insurance and retirement accounts go through probate?
what passes outside probate Washington
payable on death account probate

what goes through probate and what doesn't
Do retirement accounts (IRAs, 401ks) go through probate?
does an IRA or 401k go through probate
How do life insurance policies pay out without probate?
does life insurance go through probate
estate.a: Assets that pass by beneficiary designation, such as life insurance, retirement accounts and payable-on-death accounts, go straight to the named beneficiary. Assets held in joint tenancy pass to the surviving owner, and assets in a properly funded living trust also skip probate. What usually goes through probate is property in the person's name alone, including a house and bank accounts without beneficiary designations.
estate.pathTitle: Understanding Probate & Legal Authority

estate.q: My mom had a living trust. Does her house still have to go through probate?
alts: house in living trust probate Washington
Does a trust avoid probate for the house?
house not deeded into trust
pour-over will house not in trust
estate.a: Usually not, if the house was deeded into the trust before the death. The successor trustee takes over and can sell it, usually by giving the title company a certification of trust. But check the deed: signing a trust does not move the house into it. A house left in her own name usually goes through probate first, even when a will sends everything to the trust.
estate.pathTitle: The House Is in a Living Trust

estate.q: My parents owned the house together. Does it need probate when one of them dies?

house owned jointly with spouse probate
surviving owner house Washington
tenants in common inherited house probate
Do jointly owned assets go to probate?
does a jointly owned house go through probate
estate.a: It depends on the deed's exact wording. A house held in joint tenancy with right of survivorship belongs to the surviving owner, who usually records proof of the death with the county. Without survivorship language, co-owners hold shares that pass through each owner's estate. A married couple's community property agreement may also pass the house to the survivor without a full probate.
estate.pathTitle: The House Passed Without Probate

estate.q: We found a transfer on death deed in dad's papers. Does it work?
alts: unrecorded transfer on death deed Washington
TOD deed found after death
Does a TOD deed avoid probate?
can a will cancel a transfer on death deed
estate.a: Only if it was recorded with the county auditor before the owner's death. A transfer on death deed signed but found in a drawer afterward has no effect, and the house then usually goes through probate. A properly recorded one passes the house to the named beneficiary without probate. A will cannot revoke it; the owner had to record a revocation or new deed before death.
estate.pathTitle: Washington Probate & Estate Glossary

estate.q: What does a successor trustee do first when the trust owns the house?
alts: successor trustee first steps house
I'm trustee of mom's trust, what do I do with her house?
trustee duties real estate Washington
how to notify beneficiaries of a trust
estate.a: Confirm your authority by reading the trust and any amendments and having the trust's attorney prepare a certification of trust. Secure and insure the house, and keep paying the mortgage, taxes and utilities from trust funds. For most trusts, notify the qualified beneficiaries within 60 days of accepting the role. Get a date-of-death appraisal, and follow the trust's instructions about selling, giving or holding the house.
estate.pathTitle: Real Estate Guidance for Trustees and Successor Trustees

estate.q: Do the beneficiaries have to approve before a trustee sells the house?
alts: trustee sell house without beneficiary consent Washington
Can my brother sell mom's trust house without asking us?
beneficiary approval trust sale
does a trustee need permission to sell
estate.a: Usually not. Washington law gives a trustee the power to sell trust property, subject to the trust's terms and the trustee's duties. The beneficiaries must be kept informed, but informing them is not the same as needing their permission. Check the trust document itself, since some trusts do require consent or name who receives the house.
estate.pathTitle: Real Estate Guidance for Trustees and Successor Trustees

estate.q: My sister and I are co-trustees and we can't agree on selling the house. What now?
alts: co-trustees disagree Washington
two trustees deadlock sale
How do co-trustees make decisions?
co-trustee won't sign listing
estate.a: Start with the trust document, which may say how co-trustees decide. If it is silent, three or more trustees may act by majority, but two trustees should plan on both signing. A trustee can send written notice of a proposed action, and a co-trustee who does not object in writing within 15 days is treated as approving. If that fails, TEDRA offers mediation and then a court petition.
estate.pathTitle: Real Estate Guidance for Trustees and Successor Trustees

estate.q: My brother is living in mom's trust house for free. Is that allowed?
alts: beneficiary living rent free in trust property
trustee sibling won't move out of trust house
Can the trust charge rent to a beneficiary living in the house?
adult child staying in parent's house after death trust
estate.a: It needs a basis. First check whether the trust gives him a right to live there. The trustee must treat all beneficiaries impartially, so free use by one while the others wait is a problem. If the trust is silent, agree in writing on a move-out date and either rent or payment of taxes, insurance and utilities. Keep a record, and ask the trust's attorney whether fair rent can be charged against his share. Legal action is the last resort.
estate.pathTitle: Real Estate Guidance for Trustees and Successor Trustees

estate.q: Is selling a house out of a trust faster than a probate sale?
alts: trust sale vs probate sale timeline
how long does a trust sale take Washington
probate vs trust which is quicker
difference between probate and trust sale
estate.a: Usually, yes. In a trust sale the house passes outside probate with no court involvement, and the trustee named in the trust has authority to sell, so a sale can sometimes proceed within weeks of the death. A probate sale first needs the court to appoint the personal representative and issue letters, which adds legal steps before the house can be sold. Either way, the trustee or executor owes fiduciary duties and needs a defensible price.
estate.pathTitle: Probate vs Trust Sale in Washington State — What's the Difference?

estate.q: Can the beneficiaries challenge a trustee who sold the house too cheap?
alts: trustee sold house below market value
beneficiary sue trustee over sale price
trustee liability low sale price Washington
how does a trustee avoid claims about the price
estate.a: Yes. Beneficiaries can challenge a trust sale if they believe the trustee breached a fiduciary duty, such as selling well below market value. A trustee who acts prudently, gets an independent valuation, exposes the house to the open market and documents the decision is generally protected. Liability arises when the file is thin: no appraisal, limited marketing, or undisclosed conflicts.
estate.pathTitle: Real Estate Guidance for Trustees and Successor Trustees

estate.q: Do we have to wait four months for creditors before selling the house?
alts: sell house before creditor period ends
can probate house sell before the estate closes
Does the house have to wait until probate is finished?
sell estate house during creditor claim period
estate.a: No. With nonintervention powers, which most Washington estates have, the personal representative can sell without a court order, and the sale does not have to wait for the creditor period to end. The house can be sold before the estate closes. Only a solvent estate qualifies for nonintervention powers.
estate.pathTitle: Washington Probate Deadlines & Key Rules

estate.q: How does selling the house work if the executor doesn't have nonintervention powers?
alts: court supervised probate sale Washington
sale without nonintervention powers
Do we need court confirmation to sell the estate house?
supervised estate house sale 90 percent appraised value
estate.a: It goes through the court. Without nonintervention powers, a sale of the house generally needs a court order, then a report of sale and the court's confirmation, unless the will itself directs or authorizes the sale. A private sale generally must bring at least 90 percent of the appraised value. Most Washington estates have nonintervention powers, which let the personal representative sell without these court steps.
estate.pathTitle: Who Has Authority to Sell Probate Property?

estate.q: Can we accept the first good offer on the estate house, or is there a court bidding process?

Does a probate house sale go to auction in court?
accepting an offer in probate
court bidding process estate sale
estate.a: It depends on the type of probate. With nonintervention powers, the personal representative can negotiate and accept an offer like a normal seller. In supervised probates, and some judicial-confirmation situations, the accepted offer may be subject to overbid at a court hearing. The estate attorney can confirm which standard applies.
estate.pathTitle: Frequently Asked Questions About Probate Real Estate

estate.q: A neighbor wants to buy my mom's house. Should I just sell it to them?

family friend wants to buy dad's house before listing
accepting an offer without listing probate
quick sale to neighbor inherited house
estate.a: Not before you know what the house is worth and have authority to sell. Accepting an offer from a neighbor or family friend without a professional valuation can mean selling for much less than the house is worth, which can create problems with beneficiaries and the court and expose the executor to claims of undervaluing the asset. Get the value first, and wait for letters before agreeing to anything.
estate.pathTitle: Can an Executor Sell a House Before Probate in Washington?

estate.q: What can I do with the house while I'm waiting for the court to appoint me?
alts: prepare house during probate before letters
things executor can do before authority

use the probate waiting period
estate.a: Quite a lot. You can secure the house, keep insurance and utilities going, document its condition, get a professional assessment of value, plan the cleanout and line up vendors. Selling, major changes and disposing of significant personal property should generally wait for authority. Planning during the wait means you can list quickly once letters are issued.
estate.pathTitle: Can an Executor Sell a House Before Probate in Washington?

estate.q: How fast can a probate house sell once the executor has authority?

how long to sell an estate home
fastest a probate property can close

estate.a: Once the executor has letters testamentary, the sale itself can move much like a standard sale. A well-prepared house in good condition in a strong market sells fastest. Houses needing major work, cleanout, title fixes or agreement among heirs take longer, and the overall probate timeline is usually longer than the sale. Starting assessment and preparation during the waiting period shortens it.
estate.pathTitle: How Long Does It Take to Sell a Probate Property?

But a sale under nonintervention powers involves no court filing, so it brings no notice. If you want to know about a sale, ask the personal representative directly.
estate.pathTitle: You Inherited a House, or a Share of One

estate.q: What title problems can hold up selling an inherited house?

liens on inherited house delay closing
marketable title inherited property
estate.a: Liens, boundary disputes, missing documents, missing heirs, an unrecorded transfer or unclear ownership history can all delay closing until resolved. The title company's preliminary report, ordered early, shows who holds record title and every lien or other matter that must be cleared. Ignoring title issues until a buyer is under contract can delay or kill a sale, so review title early.

estate.q: What are my legal duties as executor?

personal representative responsibilities
what does an executor have to do
duty of loyalty executor
What are the legal duties and responsibilities of an executor?
what is an executor responsible for
estate.a: You owe fiduciary duties to the estate and its beneficiaries. Act only in their interest, not your own or one heir's; manage assets with reasonable care; keep beneficiaries informed and account for assets, debts and distributions; carry out the will as written; and pay the estate's debts before distributing anything. Executors can be held personally liable for mistakes, which is why a probate attorney is strongly recommended.
estate.pathTitle: Understanding Your Legal Duties as Executor

estate.q: Can the executor change who gets what if the will seems unfair?

executor favoring one heir
estate.a: No. The executor's job is to carry out the will's instructions, not to interpret or override them. If the will leaves the house to one heir and the savings to another, that is what must happen, whatever the executor thinks is fair. An executor who favors one heir without proper authorization breaches the duty of loyalty and can be sued by the other beneficiaries.
estate.pathTitle: Understanding Your Legal Duties as Executor

estate.q: Does the executor get paid in Washington?

can the executor take a fee from the estate

If the will sets the compensation, that is the executor's pay unless they formally renounce it before qualifying and ask the court to set a fee. If the will is silent, the executor is entitled to what the court considers just and reasonable for the work done, so keeping a log of hours and tasks helps. Failing in your duties can reduce or eliminate the fee.

estate.q: How can heirs question the fees the executor and lawyer charged?

declaration of completion 30 days

closing the estate fees reasonable
estate.a: In most Washington estates, settled without court supervision, the executor closes the estate by filing a declaration of completion that lists fees paid to the executor, attorney, appraisers and accountants. estate.pathTitle: Understanding Your Legal Duties as Executor

estate.a: No. Keep estate money separate. Commingling funds, even temporarily and with good intentions, creates accounting problems and can expose you to personal liability. Open a dedicated estate checking account as soon as possible and run all estate income and expenses, such as the mortgage, taxes and utilities on the house, through it.
estate.pathTitle: Common Executor Mistakes — and How to Avoid Them

estate.a: No. The fees of the professionals who help settle the estate, such as the probate attorney, CPA and appraiser, are paid from the estate, not from the executor's own money. Washington probate has specific filing deadlines, so engage an attorney early, ideally within the first two weeks. The site does not refer clients to attorneys; you can confirm a lawyer's license with the Washington State Bar Association.
estate.pathTitle: Working With Professionals

estate.q: I can't handle being executor. Can I step down?

named executor doesn't want to serve
professional fiduciary to act as executor
overwhelmed executor options
estate.a: Yes. Washington law allows an executor to resign and have a successor appointed. Another option is a professional fiduciary, a licensed individual or company that serves for a fee and can handle some or all of the administration. Talk with your attorney about your options; an executor who asks for help serves the estate better than one who struggles alone.

estate.q: Can I be the executor if I live outside Washington?

nonresident personal representative

estate.a: Yes. second probate in Washington
parent died in Arizona with a house in Washington

estate.a: Escalate in order. Check with the superior court clerk whether probate was opened and who was appointed. Ask the personal representative in writing for the inventory, the plan for the house and a timeline. If there is a breach of duty or neglect, an heir can petition the court, which can remove the personal representative.

estate.q: Do all the heirs have to agree before the executor sells the house?

Heirs are entitled to information and can ask the court to step in if they think the sale breaches the personal representative's duties. estate.a: Possibly. A co-owner can file a partition action asking the court to divide the property or, if it cannot be divided fairly, order it sold and the proceeds shared. estate.q: My sister lives in mom's house and won't leave. What can the executor do?
